parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: A spherical planet has mass 8.8 × 10²⁵ kg and rotates once every 0.72 Earth days. A satellite in a circular equatorial orbit remains above the same point on the planet. Calculate its orbital radius. Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² and 1 day = 86 400 s.

evidence.question: 1bii
evidence.review: Worked answer checked against the source marking guidance; wording adapted for independent IB practice.

notes: Match the satellite period to the planet’s rotation period, then equate gravitational force to the radial resultant. Radius is measured from the planet’s centre.
The planet mass is supplied, so no gravitational-potential graph from the earlier question is needed.

fep-3d9b4cac7a611e1c-qG2:whole.text: Newton’s second law gives mi a = mg g, hence a = (mg/mi)g. Equal free-fall accelerations for different materials, with air resistance absent, show that the ratio of gravitational mass to inertial mass is the same for all bodies. Choosing consistent units makes these masses equal.
fep-3d9b4cac7a611e1c-qG2:whole.display_text:
On the Moon, a hammer and a feather are released from rest at the same height and at the same time. Both reach the surface at the same time.

Explain how this demonstrates the equivalence of gravitational mass and inertial mass.
fep-3d9b4cac7a611e1c-qG2:whole.correction: Removed the source’s mistaken historical attribution and retained the physical experiment and assessed task.
